template.tagline: Light two small hybrids, climb past 100 km, come home.
template.brief: Two small hybrid motors, fins for stability and a small science box. A hybrid burns a solid fuel grain with a liquid oxidizer, so it pushes gently for a long time instead of all at once: the rocket climbs through the thick air slowly, keeps the air load and the g low, and coasts up past the 100 km line that is commonly used as the edge of space. There is nothing to stage.

benchmark.text: Sounding rockets are short research flights: up, a few minutes of data or weightlessness, then down. A long, low-thrust burn keeps max-Q and acceleration modest, which is kinder to the payload than a short, violent solid burn. 100 km is the altitude commonly used as the boundary of space.

template.tagline: The smallest rocket that can reach orbit.
template.brief: Two kerosene/oxygen stages with a cluster of small engines below and one vacuum engine above. Carbon-composite tanks keep it light. About 200 kg to a 400 km orbit: a rideshare-sized payload, but a real orbit.

benchmark.text: Dedicated small launchers carry roughly a few hundred kilograms to low Earth orbit, letting small satellites pick their own orbit and launch date. Several fly a cluster of small kerosene engines on the first stage, some driven by electric pumps instead of turbines.

template.tagline: The workhorse: nine engines, two stages, big payload.
template.brief: Nine gas-generator kerosene engines on a 3.7 m first stage and a single vacuum engine above. Throwing the first stage away (expendable) lets it carry about 15 t to a 400 km orbit. Compare it with the reusable variant to see what landing costs.

benchmark.class: Medium-lift two-stage kerolox, nine-engine first stage
benchmark.text: The medium-lift workhorse class carries tens of tonnes to low Earth orbit. A cluster of nine engines gives engine-out tolerance and lets one engine design be mass-produced for both stages.

template.tagline: Same rocket, but the booster flies home.
template.brief: Identical to Curlew, plus landing legs, grid fins, cold-gas thrusters and 35 t of propellant held back for the landing burn. That reserve and hardware cost about 4.5 t of payload. Reuse trades payload for hardware you get to fly again.

benchmark.class: Medium-lift kerolox with propulsive first-stage landing
benchmark.text: Propulsive landing of an orbital-class booster became routine in the late 2010s. The booster keeps propellant in reserve for boost-back, entry and landing burns, which is why reusable missions carry noticeably less than expendable ones.

template.tagline: Dense fuel down low, hydrogen up high.
template.brief: A kerosene first stage does the heavy lifting through the thick air, where dense propellant keeps tanks small. Above it, a wide, light hydrogen stage with two expander engines uses its high specific impulse (about 465 s) to push a 4 t satellite toward geostationary transfer orbit.

benchmark.class: Kerolox or solid booster with a hydrogen upper stage
benchmark.text: Hydrogen/oxygen upper stages have flown since the 1960s because their efficiency pays off most where every kilogram of stage mass must be pushed to orbital speed. Their low density makes tanks large, which is why they are rarely used alone on first stages.

review: Seven kerosene engines on stage 1 (not nine): with nine, thrust over mass reached 21.8 g at stage-1 burnout and the stack broke up. Seven give liftoff TWR about 1.3 and about 17 g at burnout. The upper stage is unthrottled in the sim (about 11 g at burnout); real stages throttle or shut down early.

template.tagline: Clean-burning methane and a booster built to fly again.
template.brief: Five full-flow methane engines on a stainless-steel booster that keeps 40 t of propellant to land. Methane burns cleanly (little soot to clean out between flights) and steel is cheap and tough, at the cost of heavier tanks.

benchmark.text: In the 2020s several launch companies moved to liquid methane for reusable boosters, because it leaves little soot inside engines, is denser than hydrogen and easier to store. Many of these vehicles are still in development, so performance numbers are not settled.
